title: Why polyester is in its flop era
description:
Have a look at the label in the clothes you’re wearing today. Chances are, you’re wearing some polyester. It’s the most- produced synthetic fibre on the planet and it’s having a bit of a moment on socials. In a bad way…people are giving it up and swapping for more natural fibres.

You might’ve seen claims that polyester is linked to diseases like cancer and can cause fertility issues. But how worried should we be? Professor Mohamed Abdallah from the University of Birmingham breaks it down for us and Chelsea Coates from the What in the World team explains how we can make better clothing choices.

Instagram: @bbcwhatintheworld Email: whatintheworld@bbc.co.uk WhatsApp: +44 330 12 33 22 6 Presenter: Hannah Gelbart Producers: Chelsea Coates and Emily Horler Editor: Verity Wilde
summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討聚酯纖維在社群平台上引發的反彈，並解析其對健康與環境的真實影響。節目指出，聚酯纖維佔全球纖維產量的 59% ，因耐用與抗皺而普及，但難以降解，在環境中需長達 200 年才能分解。針對網路關於聚酯纖維危害健康的傳言，伯明罕大學教授 Mohamed Abdallah 指出，聚酯纖維在製造過程中常添加阻燃劑或內分泌干擾化學物質 EDCs ，例如 PFAS 等持久性化學物質；在運動流汗或體溫升高時，衣物釋放的微纖維可能增加皮膚吸收化學物質的風險。此外，洗衣過程釋放的微塑膠是海洋微塑膠的主要來源，洗滌一件聚酯纖維襯衫一年可能釋放約 52,000 個微塑膠顆粒。團隊成員 Chelsea Coates 建議，民眾不應盲目丟棄舊衣以免加重掩埋場負擔（每年高達 85% 紡織品進入掩埋場）或造成過度消費，而是應選擇耐用衣物、關注品牌透明度，並透過低溫洗滌、低速轉速、使用洗衣袋與避免烘乾來減少微塑膠排放。
summaryEn: In this episode of What in the World, presenter Hannah Gelbart and team member Chelsea Coates discuss the growing online backlash against polyester and investigate its health and environmental impacts. Accounting for 59% of global fiber production, polyester is widely used due to its durability and moisture resistance, but it is non-biodegradable and can take up to 200 years to decompose. Addressing health concerns, Professor Mohamed Abdallah from the University of Birmingham explains that chemical additives in synthetic fabrics—such as flame retardants, endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), and PFAS—can release microfibers that pose higher skin absorption risks during workouts when body temperature and sweat increase. Additionally, washing synthetic clothing is a major source of ocean microplastics, with a single polyester shirt releasing roughly 52,000 microplastic particles per year when washed biweekly. To address these issues without contributing to landfill waste or overconsumption, the episode advises consumers to buy durable clothes, check brand supply chain transparency, and practice gentle laundry habits—such as using lower temperatures, lower spin cycles, laundry bags, and avoiding tumble drying.
